title: The ampersand was once taught as the 27th letter of the alphabet
body: The & sign began as a ligature of the letters e and t in et, Latin for ‘and’, and can be traced to Roman cursive of the 1st century CE. In 19th-century schoolbooks in the United States and elsewhere, children recited it after Z as the alphabet’s 27th letter. A letter that was also a word, such as A or I, was read with the Latin phrase per se, ‘by itself’: ‘A per se A’. So the chant ended ‘X, Y, Z, **and per se and**’, which, slurred together, became ‘ampersand’, a word in common use by 1837.

slides.heading: How & got its name
items: Letters that were words got ‘per se’: ‘A per se A’, ‘A by itself’
The alphabet ended ‘X, Y, Z, and per se and’
Said fast, ‘and per se and’ became ‘ampersand’, in use by 1837

events.text: The et ligature appears in old Roman cursive
The Dixie Primer still lists & after Z as a letter

left.label: Roman scribes
left.text: Writing fast, they joined the e and t of et into one stroke.

right.label: Italic ampersands
right.text: In some italic typefaces the e and t are still clearly visible inside the &.

slides.heading: A Gaelic cousin
slides.text: Irish and Scottish Gaelic use a different ‘and’ sign, the Tironian et, which looks like a small 7. It survives from Tironian notes, a system of shorthand.

slides.clue: Two letters joined into one sign, as e and t were joined to make &
slides.detail: The & began as a ligature of e and t in Latin et, written fast in Roman cursive of the 1st century CE.

slides.question: What does the ‘per se’ in ‘and per se and’ mean?
slides.explanation: Letters that were also words were read ‘A per se A’, ‘A by itself’. ‘And per se and’ was slurred into ‘ampersand’.
